name: Spot the missing clarification
note: An ambiguous task, and a candidate who started coding immediately. Pick the one clarifying question that would most change the solution — not the one that's merely useful.

items.prompt: Task: 'deduplicate the user list.' The candidate immediately prompts for code that removes identical rows.
candidates: 'What counts as a duplicate — identical rows, or the same person with a different email or spelling?' The dedup key IS the problem; exact-match vs fuzzy changes the entire approach
'Which programming language should I write it in?' — a surface detail that doesn't change the logic
'Roughly how many rows are there?' — useful for performance, but it doesn't change what a duplicate is
No question is needed; 'deduplicate' has one obvious meaning
items.correct: 'What counts as a duplicate — identical rows, or the same person with a different email or spelling?' The dedup key IS the problem; exact-match vs fuzzy changes the entire approach
items.explanation: The ambiguous word ('duplicate') hides two completely different problems with different algorithms. One question disambiguates the whole design. Scale matters for performance, but not for the definition of correctness — so it's the second question, not the first.
items.principle: Clarify the word the whole solution pivots on, not the surface details.

items.prompt: Task: 'cache the API responses.' The candidate immediately writes an in-memory dict cache.
candidates: 'Can responses go stale, and for how long?' Without a freshness/eviction policy a cache is a correctness bug waiting to ship — that requirement dictates TTL, invalidation, and whether in-memory even works
'Should I use a dict or a list to store it?' — an implementation detail beneath the real question
'What variable name would you prefer for the cache?' — irrelevant to the design
No question is needed; an in-memory dict cache always works
items.correct: 'Can responses go stale, and for how long?' Without a freshness/eviction policy a cache is a correctness bug waiting to ship — that requirement dictates TTL, invalidation, and whether in-memory even works
items.explanation: The hard part of caching is invalidation, not storage. Without the staleness requirement the candidate is guessing at the one decision that makes a cache correct or dangerous — and the AI will happily produce a confident, stale-by-design cache.
items.principle: For a cache, the staleness policy is the spec; the storage is a detail.

items.prompt: In a timed round with no interviewer available to answer, the task says 'sort the results by relevance.' What's the right move?
candidates: State the assumption aloud and proceed: 'Relevance isn't defined, so I'll assume X and keep the scoring function swappable' — an un-answerable ambiguity becomes visible judgment instead of a silent guess
Pick a definition silently and implement it — asking would only waste time
Refuse to start until someone defines 'relevance' for you
Prompt the AI to decide what relevance means and accept whatever it returns
items.correct: State the assumption aloud and proceed: 'Relevance isn't defined, so I'll assume X and keep the scoring function swappable' — an un-answerable ambiguity becomes visible judgment instead of a silent guess
items.explanation: Clarification isn't only questions. When you can't ask, narrating the assumption — and isolating it so it's easy to swap — shows the same judgment and protects you if the assumption was wrong. Silent guessing and uncritically delegating the definition to the AI both forfeit the signal.
items.principle: When you can't ask, narrate the assumption — visible judgment beats a silent guess.
